paper.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
paper.abstract: Abstract Proteins are essential to life, and understanding their structure can facilitate a mechanistic understanding of their function. Through an enormous experimental effort 1–4 , the structures of around 100,000 unique proteins have been determined 5 , but this represents a small fraction of the billions of known protein sequences 6,7 . Structural coverage is bottlenecked by the months to years of painstaking effort required to determine a single protein structure. Accurate computational approaches are needed to address this gap and to enable large-scale structural bioinformatics. Predicting the three-dimensional structure that a protein will adopt based solely on its amino acid sequence—the structure prediction component of the ‘protein folding problem’ 8 —has been an important open research problem for more than 50 years 9 . Despite recent progress 10–14 , existing methods fall far short of atomic accuracy, especially when no homologous structure is available. Here we provide the first computational method that can regularly predict protein structures with atomic accuracy even in cases in which no similar structure is known. We validated an entirely redesigned version of our neural network-based model, AlphaFold, in the challenging 14th Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP14) 15 , demonstrating accuracy competitive with experimental structures in a majority of cases and greatly outperforming other methods. Underpinning the latest version of AlphaFold is a novel machine learning approach that incorporates physical and biological knowledge about protein structure, leveraging multi-sequence alignments, into the design of the deep learning algorithm.
paper.tldr: AlphaFold2 predicts protein 3D structures at atomic accuracy from sequence alone—rivaling experimental structures even without homologs—via a redesigned deep learning approach that integrates physical and evolutionary (MSA) information.
paper.why: AlphaFold is the archetype of the AI-for-biology breakthrough the user prizes: a genuinely new capability solving a 50-year-old problem, validated at scale in CASP14 against experimental structures, and immediately reusable across all of biology. Among today's slate it beats strong contenders like BioEmu and OmiCLIP on total score, with maximal novelty, generality, and field-changing impact.

summary.tldr: AlphaFold2, an end-to-end deep learning system, predicts protein 3D structure from amino acid sequence at near-experimental accuracy, winning CASP14 by a wide margin and making proteome-scale structure prediction feasible.
summary.background: Predicting 3D structure from sequence alone had been an open problem for 50 years, and prior methods fell far short of atomic accuracy whenever no homologous solved structure existed. Only ~100,000 of the billions of known protein sequences had experimental structures, so determination cost was the bottleneck for structural coverage.
summary.approach: AlphaFold2 takes a sequence, a multiple sequence alignment (MSA), and optional templates as input. A trunk of 48 Evoformer blocks jointly refines an MSA representation and a residue-pair representation (with triangle-update attention enforcing geometric consistency), then a structure module with invariant point attention directly outputs all heavy-atom coordinates, iteratively refined via 'recycling'. Training used PDB structures (cutoff April 2018) with a frame-aligned point error (FAPE) loss plus a BERT-style masked-MSA objective, followed by self-distillation on predictions for 355,993 Uniclust30 sequences; training used 128 TPUv3 cores for roughly 11 days total.
findings: On CASP14 (87 domains), AlphaFold achieved median backbone accuracy of 0.96 A r.m.s.d.95 versus 2.8 A for the next-best method, and all-atom accuracy of 1.5 A versus 3.5 A.
On 10,795 PDB chains deposited after the training cutoff, median backbone r.m.s.d.95 was 1.46 A on the 3,144-chain subset with weak or no templates.
Confidence estimates are calibrated: pLDDT correlates with true lDDT-Ca (Pearson r = 0.76) and pTM with TM-score (r = 0.85) across chains.

MSAs are critical: removing both the BFD and MGnify sequence databases dropped mean GDT by 6.1 points, and accuracy degrades below ~30 effective aligned sequences; self-distillation and recycling each improved accuracy in ablations.
Inference is fast (~1 minute for a 384-residue protein on one V100 without ensembling), enabling the companion paper's prediction of the entire human proteome.
summary.why: For a transcriptomics/multiomics researcher, this is the canonical example of converting massive unlabeled biological corpora (BFD: 2.2 billion sequences) into supervision via co-evolutionary signal, self-distillation, and calibrated uncertainty. Its pairwise-representation attention, equivariant structure modules, and per-residue confidence scoring became blueprints for subsequent biomolecular ML, and its predicted structures underpin functional annotation and interpretation of omics data.
summary.limitations: Accuracy drops sharply when the MSA is shallower than ~30 sequences and for chains whose fold is determined mainly by heterotypic contacts (e.g., bridging domains in complexes); the model predicts single chains and handles missing ligands/ions only implicitly, with Amber relaxation fixing stereochemistry but not accuracy.

also.title: Scalable emulation of protein equilibrium ensembles with generative deep learning
also.abstract: Following the sequence and structure revolutions, predicting functionally relevant protein structure changes at scale remains an outstanding challenge. We introduce BioEmu, a deep learning system that emulates protein equilibrium ensembles by generating thousands of statistically independent structures per hour on a single graphics processing unit (GPU). BioEmu integrates more than 200 milliseconds of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, static structures, and experimental protein stabilities using new training algorithms. It captures diverse functional motions—including cryptic pocket formation, local unfolding, and domain rearrangements—and predicts relative free energies with 1 kilocalorie per mole accuracy compared with millisecond-scale MD and experimental data. BioEmu provides mechanistic insights by jointly modeling structural ensembles and thermodynamic properties. This approach amortizes the cost of MD and experimental data generation, demonstrating a scalable path toward understanding and designing protein function.

also.title: A visual–omics foundation model to bridge histopathology with spatial transcriptomics
also.abstract: Artificial intelligence has revolutionized computational biology. Recent developments in omics technologies, including single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, provide detailed genomic data alongside tissue histology. However, current computational models focus on either omics or image analysis, lacking their integration. To address this, we developed OmiCLIP, a visual-omics foundation model linking hematoxylin and eosin images and transcriptomics using tissue patches from Visium data. We transformed transcriptomic data into 'sentences' by concatenating top-expressed gene symbols from each patch. We curated a dataset of 2.2 million paired tissue images and transcriptomic data across 32 organs to train OmiCLIP integrating histology and transcriptomics. Building on OmiCLIP, our Loki platform offers five key functions: tissue alignment, annotation via bulk RNA sequencing or marker genes, cell-type decomposition, image-transcriptomics retrieval and spatial transcriptomics gene expression prediction from hematoxylin and eosin-stained images. Compared with 22 state-of-the-art models on 5 simulations, and 19 public and 4 in-house experimental datasets, Loki demonstrated consistent accuracy and robustness.

summary.tldr: OmiCLIP is a CLIP-style dual-encoder foundation model aligning H&E histology patches with spatial transcriptomics 'gene sentences', trained on 2.2M paired Visium patches, powering the Loki platform with five multimodal tissue-analysis tools benchmarked against 22 SOTA methods.
summary.background: Computational models have largely developed separately for images (pathology vision-language models like CONCH/PLIP) and for omics, so no unified model integrates histology with molecular data. Building one is hard because image and gene-expression modalities must be mapped to a shared space, and infrastructure to jointly analyze sequencing data and whole-slide images was lacking.
summary.approach: The authors curated ST-bank: 2,185,571 H&E patch–transcriptome pairs from 1,007 samples across 32 organs (113 studies) of 10x Visium data, encoding each patch's transcriptome as a 'sentence' of its top-50 expressed gene symbols (Ensembl IDs converted, housekeeping genes removed, rank-based to mitigate batch effects). They fine-tuned CoCa—a ViT image encoder plus causal-masking text encoder producing 768-dim embeddings—with contrastive loss for 20 epochs on one A100. On this backbone they built Loki with five modules: Align (CPD registration on embeddings), Annotate (bulk RNA-seq or marker genes as text), Decompose (Tangram optimization on OmiCLIP embeddings), Retrieve, and PredEx (similarity-weighted sum of reference ST expression).
findings: Alignment: on ovarian carcinosarcoma, Loki reached median PCC 0.88 (ST-to-ST) and 0.86 (image-to-ST) versus PASTE 0.26, GPSA 0.43, CAST 0.71; on 8 adjacent small-intestine sections median PCC was 0.62–0.83 (ST-to-ST); Visium–Xenium slide alignment error was 0.08 mm.

Annotation: zero-shot marker-gene F1 was 0.59–0.96 across CRC7K, WSSS4LUAD, LC25000 and PatchCamelyon versus 0.03–0.34 for OpenAI CLIP; averaging Loki and PLIP similarities performed best overall (93% tumor recall on CRC7K).

Decomposition: Loki scored 1.32 (ST mode) and 1.11 (image mode) on an impact metric versus −1.82 to 0.87 for ten baselines including Tangram, Cell2location and CytoSPACE; substituting scGPT, scFoundation or GeneFormer embeddings ranked 6th–9th, and Xenium ground truth on an in-house TNBC sample validated the maps.
Retrieval: median image-to-transcriptomics similarity was 0.7–0.9, with Recall@5% of 0.117–0.186, roughly 2.3–3.2× higher than CLIP and PLIP.
PredEx: best MSE in 28/39 and best PCC in 16/39 normal-heart samples versus Hist2ST, HisToGene, BLEEP and mclSTExp, while avoiding their 300 GB+, hours-long training requirements.
summary.why: This is the first demonstration that public Visium data alone suffice to pretrain an image–omics contrastive model, and that marker genes can act as labels in place of natural language. For multiomics researchers it offers a shared 768-dim embedding space where new modalities—scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq, marker lists, even proteomics—can in principle be projected and combined with pathology images without retraining.
summary.limitations: With 2.2M pairs, the training set is far smaller than billion-scale vision-language corpora, and rare conditions are underrepresented (fine-tuning is recommended for alignment and decomposition). OmiCLIP is contrastive, not generative: PredEx retrieves or similarity-weights reference expression rather than predicting transcriptomes de novo.

also.title: Predicting transcriptional outcomes of novel multigene perturbations with GEARS
also.abstract: Understanding cellular responses to genetic perturbation is central to numerous biomedical applications, from identifying genetic interactions involved in cancer to developing methods for regenerative medicine. However, the combinatorial explosion in the number of possible multigene perturbations severely limits experimental interrogation. Here, we present graph-enhanced gene activation and repression simulator (GEARS), a method that integrates deep learning with a knowledge graph of gene-gene relationships to predict transcriptional responses to both single and multigene perturbations using single-cell RNA-sequencing data from perturbational screens. GEARS is able to predict outcomes of perturbing combinations consisting of genes that were never experimentally perturbed. GEARS exhibited 40% higher precision than existing approaches in predicting four distinct genetic interaction subtypes in a combinatorial perturbation screen and identified the strongest interactions twice as well as prior approaches. Overall, GEARS can predict phenotypically distinct effects of multigene perturbations and thus guide the design of perturbational experiments.

summary.tldr: GEARS is a graph neural network model that predicts post-perturbation gene expression for single-gene and two-gene CRISPR perturbations, including combinations involving genes never perturbed in the training data.
summary.background: Perturb-seq screens measure transcriptional responses to genetic perturbation, but possible multigene combinations grow combinatorially so most can never be measured. Existing computational predictors either require each gene in a combination to have been individually perturbed before, or assume additive effects and therefore cannot capture non-additive interactions like synergy.
summary.approach: GEARS gives each gene two learned embeddings: a gene embedding refined via a gene coexpression graph, and a perturbation embedding refined via a Gene Ontology pathway-similarity graph, processed with graph neural networks. Perturbation embeddings for the genes in a set are summed and applied to each gene embedding, then a cross-gene layer and gene-specific decoders output post-perturbation expression. Training uses an 'autofocus' loss that upweights differentially expressed genes plus a direction-aware loss, and the model outputs an uncertainty score. Because unmeasured genes are still connected through the GO graph, GEARS can extrapolate to never-perturbed genes and non-additive combination effects.
findings: On single-gene Perturb-seq data (1,543 perturbations in RPE-1 and 1,092 in K562, each with over 170,000 cells), GEARS improved MSE on the top-20 differentially expressed genes by 30-50% over baselines (CPA, a CellOracle-style network-propagation model, and a no-perturbation baseline) and more than doubled Pearson correlation across all genes.

On the Norman et al. dataset (131 two-gene perturbations), GEARS improved prediction by over 30% across all generalization settings, with the largest gain (53%) when both genes in a combination were unseen during training.

For genetic interaction prediction, GEARS improved precision@10 by more than 40% for four of five subtypes (over 90% for redundancy and epistasis), ranked the ten strongest interactions about twice as accurately, and reached R^2 of roughly 0.4 for synergy/neomorphism/redundancy interaction scores versus about 0.0 for CPA.

Trained on 102 genes from Norman et al. (102 single plus 128 double perturbations), GEARS predicted all 5,151 pairwise combinations, recovered known phenotypic clusters, and predicted a new erythroid-marker-high cluster resembling proerythroblasts from the Tabula Sapiens atlas.

Against an independent cell fitness screen covering 92 gene pairs, predicted scores were higher for synergistic growth effects (P < 0.0013, n = 123) and lower for buffering effects (P < 4e-5, n = 69); directly predicting fitness gave R^2 of 0.64-0.93.
summary.why: For perturbation modeling, GEARS is a widely cited (348 citations) reference point showing that injecting prior knowledge (coexpression, GO) into a GNN enables extrapolation to unmeasured perturbations rather than only interpolation. It is a practical tool for prioritizing combinatorial CRISPR experiments and a standard baseline to benchmark newer perturbation prediction and foundation models against.
summary.limitations: GEARS must be trained on the same cell type or condition it is applied to, requires combinatorial training data to predict multigene effects well, and performs poorly for genes that are poorly connected in the knowledge graph (partially mitigated by its uncertainty output). Several predictions, including the new erythroid phenotype, remain experimentally unvalidated.
